ori_prompt: Who owns the largest share of the Vancouver Whitecaps FC?
context: Vancouver Whitecaps FC is owned by a group of four investors: Greg Kerfoot, Steve Luczo, Jeff Mallett, and Steve Nash. The group has a collective net worth over $2 billion. Kerfoot has been the majority owner of the Whitecaps since 2002, when he saved the club from contraction after previous owner David Stadnyk left the club, selling it to United Soccer Leagues. Mallett, a former chief operating officer (COO) of Yahoo!, who was raised in Victoria, British Columbia, and played for several collegiate soccer teams. He later purchased minority stakes in the San Francisco Giants of Major League Baseball and English soccer club Derby County F.C. Having first met at a charity soccer event in 2005, Mallett partnered with Steve Nash—a two-time National Basketball Association (NBA) Most Valuable Player who was also raised in Victoria—to put together a bid for a minority share of English soccer club Tottenham Hotspur F.C. in 2008. After that transaction fell through, the duo contacted Kerfoot about a minority stake in the club. Nash is the older brother of former Whitecaps midfielder Martin Nash. The fourth partner, Steve Luczo, is the president, chairman, and CEO of Seagate Technology and a partner in Boston Basketball Partners L.L.C., a group who own the NBA Boston Celtics. Luczo met Kerfoot while the two were both employed by Seagate Technology, and Kerfoot contacted Luczo proposing he become part of the club's MLS bid. In 2009, the group paid a $35 million expansion fee to MLS for the right to join the league.

ori_prompt: Is the Jakobshorn in Davos worth a trip
context:
The Jakobshorn (2,590 metres (8,500 ft)) is a mountain of the Albula Alps, overlooking Davos in the Swiss canton of Graubünden. It is also one of the five skiing regions of the Davos Klosters Mountains, offering 14 pistes.


Jakobshorn panorama
Located at the northern end of the range between the Dischmatal and Sertigtal, the Jakobshorn is served by a two-part cable car running from Davos Platz. Once on the mountain there are three chairlifts, one short cable car, and one T-Bar. Since 1995 there has also been a two-person chair-lift, running from near the base station to the near the bottom of Usser Isch.

There are a variety of pistes on the Jakobshorn—blue, red and black—and the mountain is renowned for being a centre for snowboarding; Bolgen provides an illuminated super pipe.

Pistes are very wide and the area is popular with novice skiers, there are however a number of black terrains for the more adventurous skier. The main two lifts also open during the summer, from July–October, and there are many walks on the Jakobshorn.

The Jakobshorn is also a favoured take-off point for hang-gliders and snowkiters.

ori_prompt: List all the people mentioned in this paragraph on the history of Unix
context:
The new operating system was initially without organizational backing, and also without a name. At this stage, the new operating system was a singletasking operating system, not a multitasking one such as Multics. The name Unics (Uniplexed Information and Computing Service, pronounced as "eunuchs"), a pun on Multics (Multiplexed Information and Computer Services), was initially suggested for the project in 1970. Brian Kernighan claims the coining for himself, and adds that "no one can remember" who came up with the final spelling Unix. Dennis Ritchie and Doug McIlroy also credit Kernighan.

When the Computing Sciences Research Center wanted to use Unix on a machine larger than the PDP-7, while another department needed a word processor, Thompson and Ritchie added text processing capabilities to Unix and received funding for a PDP-11. For the first time in 1970, the Unix operating system was officially named and ran on the PDP-11. A text-formatting program called roff and a text editor were added. All three were written in PDP-11 assembly language. Bell Labs used this initial text-processing system, consisting of Unix, roff, and the editor, for text processing of patent applications. Roff soon evolved into troff, the first electronic publishing program with full typesetting capability.

As the system grew in complexity and the research team wanted more users, the need for a manual grew apparent. The UNIX Programmer's Manual was published on 3 November 1971; commands were documented in the "man page" format that is still used, offering terse reference information about usage as well as bugs in the software, and listing the authors of programs to channel questions to them.

After other Bell Labs departments purchased DEC PDP-11s, they also chose to run Unix instead of DEC's own operating system. By Version 4 it was widely used within the laboratory and a Unix Support Group was formed, helping the operating system survive by formalizing its distribution.

In 1973, Version 4 Unix was rewritten in the higher-level language C, contrary to the general notion at the time that an operating system's complexity and sophistication required it to be written in assembly language. The C language appeared as part of Version 2. Thompson and Ritchie were so influential on early Unix that McIlroy estimated that they wrote and debugged about 100,000 lines of code that year, stating that "[their names] may safely be assumed to be attached to almost everything not otherwise attributed". Although assembly did not disappear from the man pages until Version 8, the migration to C suggested portability of the software, requiring only a relatively small amount of machine-dependent code to be replaced when porting Unix to other computing platforms. Version 4 Unix, however, still had considerable PDP-11-dependent code and was not suitable for porting. The first port to other platform was made five years later (1978) for Interdata 8/32.

The Unix operating system was first presented formally to the outside world at the 1973 Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, where Ritchie and Thompson delivered a paper. This led to requests for the system, but under a 1956 consent decree in settlement of an antitrust case, the Bell System (the parent organization of Bell Labs) was forbidden from entering any business other than "common carrier communications services", and was required to license any patents it had upon request. Unix could not, therefore, be turned into a product. Bell Labs instead shipped the system for the cost of media and shipping. Ken Thompson quietly began answering requests by shipping out tapes and disks, each accompanied by – according to legend – a note signed, "Love, Ken".
expected_response:
- Brian Kernighan
- Dennis Ritchie
- Doug McIlroy
- Ken Thompson

*   **Origins (1987):** Developed by Square (now Square Enix) under Hironobu Sakaguchi, *Final Fantasy* was initially conceived as a revolutionary RPG for the Famicom (Nintendo Entertainment System). It aimed to move away from the dungeon-crawling focus of earlier RPGs.

*   **Development Timeline:**
    *   **1987:** *Final Fantasy* is released in Japan.
    *   **1990:** *Final Fantasy II* expands on the formula.
    *   **1991-1994:** The “Classic” trilogy (*III*, *IV*, *V*) establishes core gameplay and story elements.
    *   **1996:** *Final Fantasy VI* (released as *Final Fantasy III* in the US) is considered a high point for storytelling and music.
    *   **1997-2000s:**  The “3D era” begins with *Final Fantasy VII*, revolutionizing the series with 3D graphics and cinematic storytelling. Subsequent games continued to innovate.

*   **Key Development Team:**
    *   **Hironobu Sakaguchi:** Producer and creator of the series.
    *   **Yoshinori Kitase:**  Lead designer and writer for many key titles (VII, X, XII, XVI).
    *   **Nobuo Uematsu:** Composer, responsible for iconic soundtracks.
    *   **Motomu Toriyama:**  Director of *Final Fantasy VII*, a pivotal game in the series’ history.

*   **Hironobu Sakaguchi:** Considered the “father” of Final Fantasy, he spearheaded the original project at Square (now Square Enix) in 1987. He envisioned a role-playing game with a strong narrative and character development, moving away from the prevalent dungeon crawling of the time.

*   **Early Development (Square):** The initial concept was a revolutionary, open-world RPG, but technical limitations forced a shift to a more structured, linear design.

*   **Final Fantasy I (1987):** The first game, despite its limitations, was a success and established the core gameplay loop.

*   **Shift to SquareSoft (1993):** The company rebranded as SquareSoft to reflect its growing international success.

*   **Key Figures in Later Games:**
    *   **Yoshinori Kitase:**  A crucial producer and writer across many titles, particularly known for *Final Fantasy VI*, *VII*, *IX*, and *X*.
    *   **Nobuo Uematsu:** The iconic composer responsible for the unforgettable soundtracks of nearly every Final Fantasy game.
    *   **Motomu Toriyama:**  A key designer and director, notably involved in *Final Fantasy VII* and *X*.

*   **Evolution & Innovation:** Subsequent games built upon the foundation, introducing new gameplay mechanics, story elements, and visual styles, solidifying Final Fantasy’s place as a landmark franchise.

rbpo_response:
A 4x4, also known as a four-wheel drive (4WD) or all-wheel drive (AWD), is a vehicle system that sends power to all four wheels simultaneously. 

**How it works:**

*   **Transfer Case:** This is the heart of the system. It splits the engine's power between the front and rear axles.
*   **Front and Rear Differentials:** These allow each axle to rotate at different speeds, which is crucial for turning.
*   **Modes:** 4x4 systems typically have modes like:
    *   **2WD (Two-Wheel Drive):** Power goes only to the front or rear wheels (depending on the vehicle). This is for normal driving.
    *   **4WD (Part-Time 4WD):** Manually engaged for low-traction situations like snow or mud. Requires driver intervention.
    *   **AWD (Automatic 4WD):** Automatically engages when the system detects slippage.

**Essentially, it provides better traction and stability by distributing power to all wheels, especially when one or more wheels lose grip.**

A 4x4 vehicle, short for four-wheel drive, is a vehicle with a drivetrain that can send power to all four wheels. Here’s a breakdown:

**Characteristics:**

*   **Drivetrain:** Typically includes a transfer case that allows the driver to switch between two-wheel drive (2WD) and four-wheel drive (4WD) modes.
*   **Differentials:**  Features multiple differentials (usually a low-range differential) to allow each wheel on an axle to rotate at different speeds – crucial for navigating uneven terrain.
*   **Increased Ground Clearance:** Generally has higher ground clearance than standard vehicles.
*   **Robust Construction:** Often built with stronger frames and components to handle tougher conditions.

**Common Uses:**

*   **Off-Roading:**  Excellent for trails, mud, snow, and rocky terrain.
*   **Towing:**  Provides better traction when towing heavy loads.
*   **Work Vehicles:** Used in construction, agriculture, and other industries requiring durability and capability.
*   **Snowy/Icy Conditions:**  Improved traction in slippery weather.

**Pros of Subleasing:**

* **Reduced Financial Burden:** Avoids the costs associated with breaking a lease (often hefty fees).

* **Potential for a Longer-Term Solution:** A good subtenant could potentially become a permanent tenant when you return.


**Rights and Obligations of Sublessees:**

* **Rights:** Sublessees generally have the same rights as the original tenant regarding quiet enjoyment, habitability, and safety, as outlined in the lease agreement. They are entitled to use the property for the agreed-upon purpose.

    * **Pay Rent on Time:**  This is paramount.

    * **Follow Lease Rules:**  They must adhere to all rules outlined in the original lease (e.g., pet policies, noise restrictions).
    * **Notify Landlord:** They must inform the landlord of any significant issues or repairs needed.
    * **Liability:** They are generally liable for their guests’ actions.



**Potential Drawbacks:**

* **Landlord Approval Required:**  You *must* get your landlord’s permission to sublease.  They can deny the request for legitimate reasons (e.g., a bad credit history of the subtenant).
* **Liability:** You remain ultimately responsible for the lease if the subtenant defaults on rent or damages the property.  Landlords can still pursue you.
* **Complex Legalities:** Subleasing can be legally complex.  It’s crucial to have a written sublease agreement drafted by a legal professional to protect both you and the subtenant.
* **Screening Responsibility:** While you screen, you're still responsible for the subtenant's actions.
* **Potential for Disputes:** Conflicts can arise between you and the subtenant, or between the subtenant and the landlord.

ori_prompt: Tell me about Hong Kong
context:
Hong Kong, officially the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China (abbr. Hong Kong SAR or HKSAR), is a city and special administrative region of China on the eastern Pearl River Delta in South China. With 7.5 million residents of various nationalities in a 1,104-square-kilometre (426 sq mi) territory, Hong Kong is one of the most densely populated places in the world. Hong Kong is also a major global financial centre and one of the most developed cities in the world.

Hong Kong was established as a colony of the British Empire after the Qing Empire ceded Hong Kong Island from Xin'an County at the end of the First Opium War in 1841 then again in 1842. The colony expanded to the Kowloon Peninsula in 1860 after the Second Opium War and was further extended when Britain obtained a 99-year lease of the New Territories in 1898. British Hong Kong was occupied by Imperial Japan from 1941 to 1945 during World War II; British administration resumed after the surrender of Japan. The whole territory was transferred to China in 1997. As one of China's two special administrative regions (the other being Macau), Hong Kong maintains separate governing and economic systems from that of mainland China under the principle of "one country, two systems".

Originally a sparsely populated area of farming and fishing villages, the territory has become one of the world's most significant financial centres and commercial ports. As of 2021, it is the world's ninth-largest exporter and eight-largest importer. Hong Kong has a market economy characterised by a focus on services, low taxation and free trade; its currency, the Hong Kong dollar, is the eighth most traded currency in the world. Hong Kong is home to the third-highest number of billionaires of any city in the world, the second-highest number of billionaires of any city in Asia, and the largest concentration of ultra high-net-worth individuals of any city in the world. Although the city has one of the highest per capita incomes in the world, severe income inequality exists among the population. Most notably, housing in Hong Kong has been well-documented to experience a chronic persistent shortage; the extremely compact house sizes and the extremely high housing density are the effects of Hong Kong's housing market being the most expensive housing in the world.

Hong Kong is a highly developed territory and has a Human Development Index (HDI) of 0.952, ranking fourth in the world. The city has the largest number of skyscrapers of any city in the world, and its residents have some of the highest life expectancies in the world. The dense space has led to a highly developed transportation network with public transport rates exceeding 90%. Hong Kong is ranked 3rd in the Global Financial Centres Index.

James Hill "Hamish" Barber FRCGP (28 May 1933 – 26 August 2007) was a doctor and medical academic. He was the first professor of general practice at the University of Glasgow and wrote the first comprehensive textbook in this field.

Early life
Barber was born on 28 May 1933 in Dunfermline, Scotland.

Medical career
Barber qualified from the University of Edinburgh in 1957. He gained a MD in 1966 with a thesis entitled A Study of Asymptomatic Bacteriuria in General Practice.

In 1972 he was appointed as senior lecturer in the organisation of medical care at the University of Glasgow. In 1974 he became the first professor of General Practice at the University. Computer-assisted learning was introduced during his tenure.

Together with Andrew Boddy, he wrote The Textbook of General Practice Medicine which was published in 1975. At just over 350 pages it was the first comprehensive textbook of this specialty.

He retired in 1993.

Later life and death
He made model boats and wrote a book on the topic that was published in 2005: Scottish fishing vessels of the nineteenth century, a guide to building scale model boats.

After a long illness, he died on 26 August 2007.

**Origins & Significance:**

*   **Ancient Roots:** Holi has deep roots in ancient Hindu mythology. It’s primarily linked to two key stories:

    *   **Narasimha Narayana Victory:** It commemorates the triumph of Vishnu in his Narasimha (half-man, half-lion) form over the demon Hiranyakashipu, representing the victory of good over evil and darkness over light. *   **Indian Subcontinent (Dominant Origin):**

    *   **Rangwali Holi:** The next day is filled with playful throwing of colored powders (gulal) and water, signifying joy, friendship, and the breaking down of social barriers.
    *   **Regional Differences:**
        *   **Punjab:** Known for *Balle Balle*, a boisterous celebration with loud music and playful attacks with colored powder.
        *   **Gujarat:** *Shobha Yatra* processions with elaborate floats and music are common.
        *   **Rajasthan:**  Celebrated with intense, chaotic, and energetic color throwing, often involving water guns and playful aggression.
*   **Global Spread (Diaspora Influence):**
    *   **Indian Diaspora:** Holi is now celebrated globally by Indian communities, often with a blend of traditional practices and local adaptations.
    *   **Western World:** Celebrations often involve community gatherings, colorful events, and a focus on friendship and inclusivity.  It’s increasingly seen as a secular festival of spring and joy.
    *   **Other Asian Countries:** In countries like Nepal, Malaysia, and Singapore, Holi is celebrated with similar themes of color and renewal, often incorporating local traditions.

**Overall Significance:**

Holi transcends religious boundaries, becoming a festival of unity, joy, and the renewal of life. It’s a time for letting go of the past, embracing new beginnings, and celebrating the vibrant spirit of community.

ori_prompt: Extract best tourist attractions in Karnataka
context:
By virtue of its varied geography and long history, Karnataka hosts numerous spots of interest for tourists. There is an array of ancient sculptured temples, modern cities, scenic hill ranges, forests and beaches. Karnataka has been ranked as the fourth most popular destination for tourism among the states of India. Karnataka has the second highest number of nationally protected monuments in India, second only to Uttar Pradesh, in addition to 752 monuments protected by the State Directorate of Archaeology and Museums. Another 25,000 monuments are yet to receive protection.

The districts of the Western Ghats and the southern districts of the state have popular eco-tourism locations including Kudremukh, Madikeri and Agumbe. Karnataka has 25 wildlife sanctuaries and five national parks. Popular among them are Bandipura National Park, Bannerghatta National Park and Nagarhole National Park. The ruins of the Vijayanagara Empire at Hampi and the monuments of Pattadakal are on the list of UNESCO's World Heritage Sites. The cave temples at Badami and the rock-cut temples at Aihole representing the Badami Chalukyan style of architecture are also popular tourist destinations. The Hoysala temples at Beluru and Halebidu, which were built with Chloritic schist (soapstone) are proposed UNESCO World Heritage sites. The Gol Gumbaz and Ibrahim Rauza are famous examples of the Deccan Sultanate style of architecture. The monolith of Gomateshwara Bahubali at Shravanabelagola is the tallest sculpted monolith in the world, attracting tens of thousands of pilgrims during the Mahamastakabhisheka festival.

Golden 5-storey Mysore Palace building with 21 domed towers and central spire
Mysore Palace in the evening, the official residence and seat of the Wodeyar dynasty, the rulers of Mysore of the Mysore Kingdom, the royal family of Mysore.
The waterfalls of Karnataka and Kudremukh are considered by some to be among the "1001 Natural Wonders of the World". Jog Falls is India's tallest single-tiered waterfall with Gokak Falls, Unchalli Falls, Magod Falls, Abbey Falls and Shivanasamudra Falls among other popular waterfalls.

Several popular beaches dot the coastline, including Murudeshwara, Gokarna, Malpe and Karwar. In addition, Karnataka is home to several places of religious importance. Several Hindu temples including the famous Udupi Sri Krishna Matha, the Marikamba Temple at Sirsi, the Kollur Mookambika Temple, the Sri Manjunatha Temple at Dharmasthala, Kukke Subramanya Temple, Janardhana and Mahakali Temple at Ambalpadi, Sharadamba Temple at Shringeri attract pilgrims from all over India. Most of the holy sites of Lingayatism, like Kudalasangama and Basavana Bagewadi, are found in northern parts of the state. Shravanabelagola, Mudabidri and Karkala are famous for Jain history and monuments. Jainism had a stronghold in Karnataka in the early medieval period with Shravanabelagola as its most important centre. The Shettihalli Rosary Church near Shettihalli, an example of French colonial Gothic architecture, is a rare example of a Christian ruin, is a popular tourist site.

Karnataka has become a center of health care tourism and has the highest number of approved health systems and alternative therapies in India. Along with some ISO certified government-owned hospitals, private institutions which provide international-quality services, Hospitals in Karnataka treat around 8,000 health tourists every year.

bpo_response:
Okay, here’s a detailed explanation of the Counter-Reformation:

**What was the Counter-Reformation?**

The Counter-Reformation (roughly 1545-1648) was the Catholic Church’s response to the Protestant Reformation of the 16th century. It wasn’t simply a defensive reaction; it was a proactive effort to revitalize the Church, reaffirm Catholic doctrine, and regain lost ground.

**Main Features & Strategies:**

1. **The Council of Trent (1545-1563):** This was the central event. It addressed criticisms of the Church and defined Catholic doctrine more clearly. Key outcomes included:
   * **Reaffirmation of Traditional Doctrine:**  The Council reaffirmed the seven sacraments, the authority of the Pope, transubstantiation (the belief that bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ), and the importance of good works alongside faith.
   * **Church Reform:**  It addressed corruption within the Church – addressing simony (buying and selling church offices), clerical immorality, and abuses of indulgences.
   * **Improved Education:**  Established seminaries to train better-educated priests.

2. **The Society of Jesus (Jesuits) (1540):** Founded by Ignatius of Loyola, the Jesuits were a highly disciplined and effective religious order. They played a crucial role in:
   * **Education:** They established schools and universities throughout Europe to spread Catholic teachings.
   * **Missionary Work:** They were incredibly successful in converting indigenous populations in the Americas, Asia, and Africa.
   * **Defense of the Faith:** They actively combatted Protestant ideas and defended Catholic doctrine.

3. **The Inquisition:**  Reinforced and expanded, the Inquisition was used to investigate and punish heresy.  It wasn't just about punishment; it also aimed to root out dissent and maintain religious uniformity.  It operated differently in various regions, with varying levels of severity.

4. **Art and Propaganda:** The Church recognized the power of visual and written communication.
   * **Baroque Art:**  A dramatic, emotional style of art was promoted to inspire religious fervor.
   * **Pamphlets and Prints:**  Used to disseminate Catholic ideas and refute Protestant arguments.


**Impact on the Catholic Church:**

* **Strengthened Authority:** The Counter-Reformation significantly bolstered the authority of the Pope and the Catholic hierarchy.
* **Reduced Protestant Gains:** While it didn't completely reverse the Reformation, it halted the spread of Protestantism in many areas and solidified Catholic control in regions like Italy and Spain.
* **Increased Religious Unity:**  It created a more unified and disciplined Catholic Church, less susceptible to internal divisions.
* **Shift in Religious Landscape:**  The Counter-Reformation led to a more conservative and orthodox Catholicism, distinct from the more radical forms of Protestantism.
* **Long-Term Division:**  Despite its successes, the Counter-Reformation ultimately contributed to the long-term division between Catholics and Protestants, solidifying the religious landscape of Europe.

**What was the Counter-Reformation?**

The Counter-Reformation (roughly 1545-1648) was the Catholic Church’s response to the Protestant Reformation of the 16th century. It wasn’t simply a defensive reaction; it was a proactive movement aimed at reforming the Church from within and combating the spread of Protestantism.

**Key Objectives:**

* **Stemming the Spread of Protestantism:** The primary goal was to halt the growth of Lutheranism, Calvinism, and other Protestant denominations.
* **Reforming Church Practices:**  Recognizing internal corruption and abuses (like the sale of indulgences), the Church aimed to purify itself and restore traditional Catholic doctrines and practices.
* **Renewing Religious Zeal:**  To revitalize Catholic faith and piety among European populations.
* **Reasserting Papal Authority:**  To reaffirm the Pope’s supreme authority over the Church and Christendom.


**Major Figures:**

* **Pope Paul III (1534-1549):**  Called the Council of Trent, the central event of the Counter-Reformation.
* **Cardinal Lorenzo Girolamo Savonarola (1494-1527):**  A Dominican friar who briefly led Florence after the expulsion of the Medici, known for his puritanical reforms and public burnings of "vanities." (Though his time was earlier, his influence shaped the movement’s tone.)
* **Ignatius of Loyola (1491-1556):** Founder of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits), a highly disciplined and effective order dedicated to education, missionary work, and combating heresy.
* **St. Teresa of Ávila (1515-1582) & St. John of the Cross (1542-1591):** Carmelite nuns who reformed their order with stricter rules and a focus on mystical prayer.
* **Charles Borromeo (1538-1584):** Archbishop of Milan, known for his efforts to reform the clergy and promote piety in his diocese.



**Significant Impacts (16th & 17th Centuries):**

* **Council of Trent (1545-1563):** This council was *the* defining event. It:
    * **Reaffirmed Catholic Doctrine:**  Reiterated traditional beliefs on the sacraments, the authority of Scripture and Tradition, and the role of the Church.
    * **Reformed Church Practices:**  Ended the sale of indulgences, reformed clerical education, and established stricter standards for priestly ordination.
    * **Established the Index Librorum Prohibitorum:** A list of books banned for containing heretical or dangerous ideas.
* **The Society of Jesus (Jesuits):**  The Jesuits were incredibly successful:
    * **Education:** Established schools and universities throughout Europe and the Americas, promoting Catholic education.
    * **Missionary Work:**  Spread Catholicism to Asia, Africa, and the Americas.
    * **Political Influence:**  Worked to influence European politics in favor of the papacy.
* **Religious Art & Architecture:**  The Baroque style emerged as a response to Protestant austerity, emphasizing emotional impact and grandeur to inspire religious devotion.
* **Increased Religious Persecution:**  Catholic authorities intensified efforts to suppress Protestantism, leading to witch hunts, burnings at the stake, and other forms of persecution.
* **Religious Wars:** The Counter-Reformation fueled religious conflicts across Europe, including the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648).
* **Rise of Religious Orders:**  New religious orders like the Carthusians and the Discalced Carmelites emerged, emphasizing contemplative prayer and asceticism.

**In short, the Counter-Reformation was a complex and multifaceted movement that profoundly shaped the religious, cultural, and political landscape of Europe for centuries.**

* **Shelter:** Shade is paramount.  Rock overhangs, digging shallow depressions, creating a sunshade with clothing/branches.

* **Shelter:** Sand dunes, driftwood piles, caves.

bpo_response:
Okay, here's a detailed explanation of what a SQL query is:

**A SQL query is a request for data from a database.**  Think of it like asking a question of a database.

Here's a breakdown:

* **SQL stands for Structured Query Language:** It’s the standard language used to communicate with relational databases.
* **Query:**  The "query" part is the actual question you're asking.
* **Structure:** SQL queries follow a specific structure (syntax) to tell the database *what* data you want and *how* you want it.

**Basic Components of a SQL Query:**

1. **`SELECT` Clause:**  This specifies *which* columns you want to retrieve.  Example: `SELECT name, age FROM users;` (This retrieves the 'name' and 'age' columns from a table named 'users'.)

2. **`FROM` Clause:** This specifies *which* table the data is coming from. Example: `SELECT name, age FROM users;` (As above, it’s part of the same query.)

3. **`WHERE` Clause (Optional):** This filters the data based on a condition. Example: `SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age > 25;` (This retrieves names and ages only for users older than 25.)

4. **`ORDER BY` Clause (Optional):** This sorts the results. Example: `SELECT name, age FROM users ORDER BY age DESC;` (This retrieves names and ages, sorted by age in descending order – oldest first.)

5. **`GROUP BY` Clause (Optional):** This groups rows that have the same value in one or more columns. Often used with aggregate functions (like `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`).

6. **`HAVING` Clause (Optional):**  This filters the results *after* grouping.  Similar to `WHERE`, but for grouped data.


**Example of a Complete Query:**

```sql
SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE category = 'Electronics'
ORDER BY price DESC;
```

This query retrieves the name and price of all products in the 'Electronics' category, sorted from the most expensive to the least expensive.

**Basic Syntax:**

The general structure of a SQL query is:

```sql
SELECT column1, column2, ...
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;
```

*   **SELECT:** Specifies the columns you want to retrieve.
*   **FROM:**  Specifies the table you want to retrieve data from.
*   **WHERE:** (Optional) Filters the rows based on a condition.

**Examples:**

1.  **Retrieve all columns and rows from a `customers` table:**

    ```sql
    SELECT *
    FROM customers;
    ```

2.  **Retrieve only the `name` and `email` columns from the `customers` table:**

    ```sql
    SELECT name, email
    FROM customers;
    ```

3.  **Retrieve customers from a specific city (e.g., 'New York'):**

    ```sql
    SELECT *
    FROM customers
    WHERE city = 'New York';
    ```

4.  **Retrieve customers older than 30:**

    ```sql
    SELECT *
    FROM customers
    WHERE age > 30;
    ```

5.  **Retrieve the names of customers whose email contains "gmail.com":**

    ```sql
    SELECT name
    FROM customers
    WHERE email LIKE '%gmail.com%';
    ```

**Key Concepts:**

*   **Tables:**  Data is organized in tables with rows and columns.
*   **Columns:** Represent specific attributes (e.g., name, age, city).
*   **Rows:** Represent individual records (e.g., a single customer).

Okay, let’s break down the world of pepper spiciness!

**The Scoville Scale**

The Scoville scale is how we measure the “heat” of chili peppers. It’s based on a process called “Scoville testing,” originally developed by pharmacist Wilbur Scoville in 1912. Here’s the gist:

*   **Capsaicin:** The chemical compound responsible for the heat is called capsaicin. Different peppers have different amounts of capsaicin.
*   **Dilution:** Scoville testing involves diluting a pepper extract until the heat is just barely perceptible. The number of dilutions needed to reach that point is the Scoville Heat Unit (SHU) score.  So, a pepper with a higher SHU is hotter.

**The Hottest Pepper – Pepper X**

Currently, the hottest pepper in the world, as of late 2023, is **Pepper X**. Developed by Ed Currie (of the Carolina Reaper fame) at the PuckerButt Pepper Company, it boasts an average SHU of **2.69 million**.  However, some samples have reached over 3.18 million SHU! It’s a complex hybrid of the Carolina Reaper and a pepper of unknown origin.

**Other Notable Peppers (SHU Estimates):**

*   **Carolina Reaper:** 1.64 - 2.2 million SHU (Currently the second hottest)
*   **Trinidad Moruga Scorpion:** 1.2 million - 2 million SHU
*   **7 Pot Douglah:** 923,000 - 1.86 million SHU
*   **Ghost Pepper (Bhut Jolokia):** 855,000 - 1,041,427 SHU (Previously the hottest)

**Peppers That Aren't Spicy**

Many peppers exist that have *no* heat. These are often prized for their flavor and aroma:

*   **Bell Peppers:** (Sweet Peppers) – Around 0 SHU. They come in various colors (green, red, yellow, orange) and are mild and fruity.
*   **Banana Peppers:**  Around 0 SHU.  Mild, tangy, and often pickled.
*   **Poblano Peppers:** Around 1,000 - 2,000 SHU.  Mildly spicy, often used in Mexican cuisine.
*   **Shishito Peppers:** Around 50-300 SHU.  Most are mild, but occasionally you’ll get a fiery one!

ori_prompt: What is the game called Lacrosse
expected_response:
Lacrosse is a team sport played with a lacrosse stick and a lacrosse ball. It is the oldest organized sport in North America,[ with its origins with the indigenous people of North America as early as the 12th century.The game was extensively modified by European colonists, reducing the violence, to create its current collegiate and professional form.

Players use the head of the lacrosse stick to carry, pass, catch, and shoot the ball into the goal. The sport has four versions that have different sticks, fields, rules and equipment: field lacrosse, women's lacrosse, box lacrosse and intercrosse. The men's games, field lacrosse (outdoor) and box lacrosse (indoor), are contact sports and all players wear protective gear: helmet, gloves, shoulder pads, and elbow pads. The women's game is played outdoors and does not allow body contact but does allow stick to stick contact.The only protective gear required for women players is eyegear, while goalies wear helmets and protective pads. Both men's and women's field lacrosse have 6v6 versions played on smaller fields, gaining acceptance in multi-sport events. Intercrosse is a mixed-gender non-contact sport played indoors that uses an all-plastic stick and a softer ball.

The modern sport is governed by World Lacrosse and is the only international sport organization to recognize First Nations bands and Native American tribes as sovereign nations.The organization hosts the World Lacrosse Championship for men, the Women's Lacrosse World Cup, the World Indoor Lacrosse Championship for box lacrosse, and the Under-19 World Lacrosse Championships for both men and women. Each is held every four years. Lacrosse at the Summer Olympics has been contested at two editions of the Summer Olympic Games, 1904 and 1908.It was also held as a demonstration event at the 1928, 1932, and 1948 Summer Olympics.

mepo_response:
Here’s a detailed explanation of the Crusades:

**What were the Crusades?**

The Crusades were a series of religiously motivated military campaigns primarily launched by European Christians between the late 11th and 15th centuries. They were largely sanctioned and organized by the Roman Catholic Church.

**Historical Context:**

*   **Religious Zeal:** Growing Christian fervor in Europe, fueled by the perceived threat of Islam expanding after the Islamic conquests of the 10th and 11th centuries, created a desire to reclaim the Holy Land (particularly Jerusalem).
*   **Political Factors:** European rulers sought to expand their territories, gain prestige, and divert internal conflicts outward. The papacy used the Crusades to assert its authority and unite Europe.
*   **Byzantine Appeal:** The Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) requested military assistance from the West against the Seljuk Turks, who had seized much of Anatolia (modern-day Turkey) and threatened Constantinople.

**Primary Objectives:**

*   **Reconquest of Jerusalem:** The central goal of most Crusades was to liberate Jerusalem and other Christian holy sites from Muslim control.
*   **Expansion of Christendom:** Crusaders aimed to spread Christianity and establish Christian states in the Levant (the Eastern Mediterranean).
*   **Papal Authority:** The Crusades were a means for the papacy to increase its political and spiritual influence.

**Key Events (Examples):**

*   **First Crusade (1096-1099):**  Successful capture of Jerusalem in 1099. Established Crusader states (e.g., Kingdom of Jerusalem, County of Tripoli).
*   **Second Crusade (1147-1149):**  Failed attempt to recapture Edessa.
*   **Third Crusade (1189-1192):** Led by prominent European monarchs (Richard the Lionheart, Philip II, Frederick I), resulted in the recapture of Jerusalem but not a permanent hold.
*   **Later Crusades:**  Included the Albigensian Crusade (against Catharism in Southern France), the Children's Crusade (a largely unsuccessful movement of children), and the Mamluk Crusade (a disastrous defeat by the Mamluks of Egypt).


**Major Impacts:**

*   **Europe:**
    *   **Increased Trade:**  Crusades stimulated trade between Europe and the East, introducing new goods and ideas.
    *   **Rise of Towns & Merchant Class:**  Crusader armies relied on supplies from towns, boosting their growth.
    *   **Military Innovation:**  European armies adopted new military tactics and technologies.
    *   **Religious Intolerance:**  Increased persecution of Jews and other religious minorities in Europe.
*   **Middle East:**
    *   **Political Fragmentation:**  The Crusader states created new political divisions in the Levant.
    *   **Economic Disruption:**  The Crusades caused widespread destruction and economic hardship.
    *   **Cultural Exchange:**  Despite conflict, there was some exchange of knowledge and ideas between East and West (though often limited and fraught with tension).
    *   **Rise of Islamic Unity:**  The Crusades spurred a sense of Islamic unity against a common Christian enemy.

**Decline:**

The Crusades gradually declined after the 15th century due to a combination of factors, including the Ottoman conquest of the Crusader states, the rise of centralized states in Europe, and a waning of religious fervor.

*   **Political & Economic Factors:** European rulers saw crusading as an opportunity to expand territory, gain wealth, and assert power.  The Byzantine Empire, weakened by the Seljuk Turks, appealed for help.

**Key Events & Campaigns:**

*   **First Crusade (1096-1099):** The most successful, resulting in the capture of Jerusalem in 1099. Marked by extreme violence and massacres.
*   **Second Crusade (1147-1149):** Launched in response to the fall of Edessa, it was largely unsuccessful.
*   **Third Crusade (1189-1192):** Led by prominent European monarchs (Richard the Lionheart, Philip II, Frederick I), aimed to recapture Jerusalem from Saladin.
*   **Fourth Crusade (1202-1204):**  Deviated from its original goal and sacked Constantinople, further damaging relations with the Byzantine Empire.
*   **Later Crusades:** Several smaller campaigns followed, but with diminishing success and impact.


**Major Participants:**

*   **European Kingdoms:** France, England, Holy Roman Empire, Spain, and others sent armies.
*   **Knights Templar & Hospitaller:** Religious military orders that gained immense wealth and power.
*   **Byzantine Empire:** Initially requested aid, then suffered greatly from the Fourth Crusade.
*   **Muslim States:** Primarily the Ayyubid dynasty under Saladin, who successfully defended the Holy Land.

**Lasting Impacts:**

*   **Increased Trade:** The Crusades stimulated trade between Europe and the East, introducing new goods and ideas.
*   **Cultural Exchange:**  Exposure to Eastern cultures influenced European art, architecture, and learning.
*   **Rise of Nation-States:**  The Crusades contributed to the rise of centralized monarchies in Europe.
*   **Religious Tensions:**  The Crusades deepened religious divisions between Christians and Muslims, contributing to centuries of conflict.
*   **Decline of Papal Authority:** The failures of later crusades and the Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople significantly weakened the Pope’s authority.

ori_prompt: What are some defining qualities of authoritarianism?
context:
Authoritarianism is a political system characterized by the rejection of political plurality, the use of strong central power to preserve the political status quo, and reductions in the rule of law, separation of powers, and democratic voting. Political scientists have created many typologies describing variations of authoritarian forms of government. Authoritarian regimes may be either autocratic or oligarchic and may be based upon the rule of a party or the military. States that have a blurred boundary between democracy and authoritarianism have some times been characterized as "hybrid democracies", "hybrid regimes" or "competitive authoritarian" states.

The political scientist Juan Linz, in an influential 1964 work, An Authoritarian Regime: Spain, defined authoritarianism as possessing four qualities:

Limited political pluralism, is realized with constraints on the legislature, political parties and interest groups.
Political legitimacy is based upon appeals to emotion and identification of the regime as a necessary evil to combat "easily recognizable societal problems, such as underdevelopment or insurgency."
Minimal political mobilization, and suppression of anti-regime activities.
Ill-defined executive powers, often vague and shifting extend the power of the executive.
Minimally defined, an authoritarian government lacks free and competitive direct elections to legislatures, free and competitive direct or indirect elections for executives, or both. Broadly defined, authoritarian states include countries that lack civil liberties such as freedom of religion, or countries in which the government and the opposition do not alternate in power at least once following free elections. Authoritarian states might contain nominally democratic institutions such as political parties, legislatures and elections which are managed to entrench authoritarian rule and can feature fraudulent, non-competitive elections. In contexts of democratic backsliding, scholars tend to identify authoritarian political leaders based on certain tactics, such as: politicizing independent institutions, spreading disinformation, aggrandizing executive power, quashing dissent, targeting vulnerable communities, stoking violence, and corrupting elections. Since 1946, the share of authoritarian states in the international political system increased until the mid-1970s but declined from then until the year 2000.
expected_response:
1. Limited political pluralism or outright rejection of political pluralism.
2. Lack of civil liberties
3. Lack of free, fair and competitive elections
4. So-called democratic institutions corrupted by authoritarian rule
5. Use of election tactics such as spreading misinformation, politicizing independent institutions, quashing dissent, engaging in culture wars, targeting vulnerable communities, stoking violence, and aggrandizing executive power.
6. Use of a strong central power to preserve the political status quo at the cost of basic democratic ideals such as the rule of law, separation of powers, and voting rights.

bpo_response:
Okay, here’s a detailed breakdown of the structure of a Public Forum debate as used in US debate competitions (primarily governed by the National Speech and Debate Association – NSDA):

**1. Basic Format (Round Structure):**

*   **Time Allotment:** Each round is 6 minutes total – 3 minutes for Affirmative (pro side) and 3 minutes for Negative (con side).
*   **Opening Statements (30 seconds each):**  Each team delivers a brief, high-level overview of their case.
*   **Constructive Arguments (3 minutes):** This is the core of the debate. Each team presents their main arguments, supported by evidence.
*   **Rebuttal (3 minutes):** The opposing team has the opportunity to directly respond to the arguments and evidence presented in the constructive.
*   **Close (30 seconds):**  Each team summarizes their key points and restates their position.

**2. Roles & Team Composition:**

*   **Two Teams:** Each debate consists of two teams – Affirmative and Negative.
*   **Roles:**
    *   **Speaker 1 (Affirmative):** Typically focuses on the main case and initial arguments.
    *   **Speaker 2 (Affirmative):** Often handles more complex evidence and deeper analysis.
    *   **Speaker 1 (Negative):** Primarily defends against the Affirmative’s arguments.
    *   **Speaker 2 (Negative):**  Focuses on attacking the Affirmative’s evidence and offering alternative perspectives.

**3. The Resolution:**

*   A specific topic is presented as the “resolution.”  Examples: "Resolved: The United States federal government should substantially increase its regulation of social media."
*   Both teams must argue *for* or *against* this resolution.

**4. Evidence & Research:**

*   **Evidence is Crucial:** Debate is heavily reliant on credible evidence.
*   **Types of Evidence:** Primarily uses:
    *   **Polling Data:**  Surveys and public opinion polls.
    *   **Statistical Data:**  Numbers and statistics from reputable sources.
    *   **Expert Testimony:** Quotes and analysis from recognized experts.
    *   **Legislation/Policy:**  References to laws, regulations, and government policies.
*   **Citation:**  All evidence *must* be properly cited (e.g., “Pew Research Center, 2023”).  Judges will heavily scrutinize citations.

**5. Reasoning & Logical Argumentation (The Most Important Part):**

*   **Frameworks:** Teams use pre-defined debate frameworks (e.g.,  "Kashmir," "Cross-Examination") to structure their arguments. These frameworks provide a logical sequence of steps.
*   **Logic:**  Debaters must demonstrate clear, logical connections between their evidence and their claims.  Simply presenting evidence isn't enough; they must *explain* how it supports their position.
*   **Critical Thinking:**  Debaters must anticipate the opposition’s arguments and address them proactively.
*   **Fallacies:**  Avoiding logical fallacies (e.g., ad hominem, straw man) is essential.

**6. Role of the Judges:**

*   **Evaluation Criteria:** Judges evaluate teams based on a rubric that typically includes:
    *   **Evidence:** Quality, relevance, and proper citation.
    *   **Argumentation:** Clarity, logic, and persuasiveness.
    *   **Refutation:** Effectiveness of responding to the opposition.
    *   **Delivery:**  Speaking skills, organization, and overall presentation.
*   **Judging Style:** Judges typically award points throughout the round, not just at the end. They may provide brief feedback during the debate.

*   **Time Allotment:** 6 minutes for Affirmative, 6 minutes for Negative, 3 minutes for Rebuttal (shared), and 1 minute for closing statements.

*   **Solvers:**  Specific arguments that address weaknesses in the Negative’s case or offer solutions to the problem.
*   **Refutation:** Directly challenging the Negative’s arguments and evidence.

Robert Kiyosaki is an American author and investor best known for his personal finance books, particularly *Rich Dad Poor Dad*. Here’s a detailed breakdown of his background:

**Early Life & Military Service:**

*   **Born:** September 21, 1947, in Newton, Massachusetts.
*   **Military Career:** Kiyosaki served in the U.S. Navy from 1969 to 1974. He was stationed in Vietnam and worked as a military police officer. This experience significantly shaped his views on money and authority.
*   **Early Business Ventures:** Before his books gained popularity, he had a varied and often unsuccessful career. He worked as a real estate salesman, a computer salesman, and a business consultant. He experienced significant financial losses early on, which heavily influenced the core message of his books.

**Rise to Fame with *Rich Dad Poor Dad*:**

*   **The Book's Origin:** *Rich Dad Poor Dad* (1997) was inspired by the contrasting financial philosophies of his biological father (the "poor dad," a government employee) and his best friend’s father (the "rich dad," a successful businessman).  The book contrasts these two father figures' approaches to money and investing.
*   **Key Concepts:** The book popularized concepts like:
    *   **Assets vs. Liabilities:**  Distinguishing between assets (things that put money in your pocket) and liabilities (things that take money out).
    *   **Financial Literacy:**  The importance of understanding financial statements and investing.
    *   **Mindset:**  Shifting from a job-based mentality to an investment mindset.

**Subsequent Books & Business Empire:**

*   **Follow-up Books:** He’s written several other books, including *Poor Dad Rich Dad! An Unexpected Lesson in Business* (1998), *The Late O’Shares Early Retirement* (2006), *Early Retirement Blueprint* (2011), and *Enterpreneurial Thinking* (2019).
*   **Kiyosaki Education:** He founded Kiyosaki Education, a company offering courses and seminars on financial literacy and entrepreneurship.
*   **Real Estate Investments:** Kiyosaki has been a significant real estate investor, owning numerous properties.
*   **Controversies:** He has faced criticism and controversy regarding the accuracy of some of the investment strategies he promotes and the overall claims made in his books. Some critics argue his advice is overly simplistic and potentially misleading.


**In short, Robert Kiyosaki is a self-made businessman who rose to prominence by sharing his personal financial experiences and advocating for a different approach to wealth building, emphasizing financial literacy and investing.**

4.  **Makemake:** (Dwarf Planet) – Another Kuiper Belt object, Makemake is reddish in color and has a surprisingly large, bright forward-facing lobe of atmosphere.

5.  **Haumea:** (Dwarf Planet) – Haumea is a rapidly rotating, elongated object in the Kuiper Belt. It’s unique for having a ring system and two moons.

context:
The World Bank is an international financial institution that provides loans and grants to the governments of low- and middle-income countries for the purpose of pursuing capital projects. The World Bank is the collective name for the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) and International Development Association (IDA), two of five international organizations owned by the World Bank Group. It was established along with the International Monetary Fund at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference. After a slow start, its first loan was to France in 1947. In the 1970s, it focused on loans to developing world countries, shifting away from that mission in the 1980s. For the last 30 years, it has included NGOs and environmental groups in its loan portfolio. Its loan strategy is influenced by the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals, as well as environmental and social safeguards.

As of 2022, the World Bank is run by a president and 25 executive directors, as well as 29 various vice presidents. IBRD and IDA have 189 and 174 member countries, respectively. The U.S., Japan, China, Germany and the U.K. have the most voting power. The bank aims loans at developing countries to help reduce poverty. The bank is engaged in several global partnerships and initiatives, and takes a role in working toward addressing climate change. The World Bank operates a number of training wings and it works with the Clean Air Initiative and the UN Development Business. It works within the Open Data Initiative and hosts an Open Knowledge Repository.

The World Bank has been criticized as promoting inflation and harming economic development, causing protests in 1988 and 2000. There has also been criticism of the bank's governance and response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

context:
Musk attended Waterkloof House Preparatory School, Bryanston High School, and Pretoria Boys High School, from which he graduated. Musk applied for a Canadian passport through his Canadian-born mother, knowing that it would be easier to immigrate to the United States this way. While waiting for his application to be processed, he attended the University of Pretoria for five months.

Musk arrived in Canada in June 1989 and lived with a second cousin in Saskatchewan for a year, working odd jobs at a farm and lumber mill. In 1990, he entered Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario. Two years later, he transferred to the University of Pennsylvania (UPenn), where he completed studies for a Bachelor of Arts degree in physics and a Bachelor of Science degree in economics from the Wharton School. Although Musk claims he earned the degrees in 1995, UPenn maintains it awarded them in 1997. He reportedly hosted large, ticketed house parties to help pay for tuition, and wrote a business plan for an electronic book-scanning service similar to Google Books.

In 1994, Musk held two internships in Silicon Valley: one at the energy storage startup Pinnacle Research Institute, which investigated electrolytic ultracapacitors for energy storage, and another at the Palo Alto–based startup Rocket Science Games. In 1995, he was accepted to a PhD program in materials science at Stanford University. However, Musk decided to join the Internet boom, instead dropping out two days after being accepted and applied for a job at Netscape, to which he reportedly never received a response.

Okay, here’s a concise overview of Salvador, Brazil:

**Location:** Salvador (Bahia) is located on the northeastern coast of Brazil, specifically in Bahia state. It’s the capital of Bahia.

*   **Early History (1549):** Founded as *Vila da Bahia* by the Portuguese in 1549, it was the first capital of Brazil. It was strategically important for trade and colonization.
*   **Capital of Brazil (1763-1967):** Salvador served as the capital of Brazil for over two centuries, a period marked by significant wealth from the sugar trade and a complex social structure with a large population of enslaved Africans.
*   **African Heritage:** Salvador is renowned for its strong Afro-Brazilian culture, deeply rooted in its history as a major port for the transatlantic slave trade. This is reflected in its music (samba, axé), religion (Candomblé and Umbanda), cuisine, and architecture.
*   **Pelourinho:** The historic center, *Pelourinho*, is a UNESCO World Heritage site, showcasing colonial architecture and a vibrant cultural scene. It was once the site of a slave market (Pelourinho means "skull place").
*   **Modern Era:**  Salvador transitioned from a colonial power to a modern city, retaining its unique cultural identity.


**In short:** Salvador is a historically significant city with a rich Afro-Brazilian culture, shaped by its role as Brazil’s first capital and a major port for the slave trade.

*   **Proprioception:**  Reduced awareness of body position can cause errors.

No, it’s generally *not* considered wrong to split the infinitive in English. However, it’s often viewed as less formal and sometimes stylistically awkward. Here’s a detailed explanation:

**What is an Infinitive?**

An infinitive is the base form of a verb, usually preceded by “to,” like “to run,” “to eat,” or “to think.”  The infinitive phrase is “to + verb.”

**The Rule (and its Relaxing):**

Traditionally, English grammar dictated that you *never* split an infinitive – you always said “to run” and never “running.” This rule stems from Latin grammar, where infinitives are treated differently.

**Why the Rule is Now Relaxed:**

* **Modern Usage:**  Over time, English has become more flexible.  Splitting infinitives is now widely accepted and common, especially in informal speech and writing.
* **Clarity and Emphasis:** Splitting an infinitive can sometimes make a sentence clearer or more emphatic.  It can highlight the specific action you want to emphasize.
* **Natural Sounding:**  Sometimes, a split infinitive simply sounds more natural than trying to rephrase the sentence to avoid it.


**When to Avoid Splitting (Generally):**

* **Formal Writing:** In academic papers, legal documents, or very formal writing, it’s best to avoid splitting infinitives.
* **When it Creates Awkwardness:** If splitting the infinitive makes the sentence convoluted or difficult to understand, it’s better to rephrase.

**Examples:**

* **Correct (Traditional):** “I want to quickly finish the report.”
* **Acceptable (Split):** “I want to quickly finish the report.” (Often preferred for emphasis)
* **Potentially Awkward (Avoid):** “I want finishing the report quickly.”


**In short:** While the traditional rule exists, it’s largely a matter of style.  Splitting infinitives is now frequently acceptable, particularly in less formal contexts, and can often improve clarity.

ori_prompt: Using examples taken from the text give me a rundown of the primary environments found in Yellowstone National Park.
context:
Yellowstone National Park is an American national park located in the western United States, largely in the northwest corner of Wyoming and extending into Montana and Idaho. It was established by the 42nd U.S. Congress with the Yellowstone National Park Protection Act and signed into law by President Ulysses S. Grant on March 1, 1872. Yellowstone was the first national park in the U.S. and is also widely held to be the first national park in the world. The park is known for its wildlife and its many geothermal features, especially the Old Faithful geyser, one of its most popular. While it represents many types of biomes, the subalpine forest is the most abundant. It is part of the South Central Rockies forests ecoregion.

While Native Americans have lived in the Yellowstone region for at least 11,000 years, aside from visits by mountain men during the early-to-mid-19th century, organized exploration did not begin until the late 1860s. Management and control of the park originally fell under the jurisdiction of the U.S. Department of the Interior, the first Secretary of the Interior to supervise the park being Columbus Delano. However, the U.S. Army was eventually commissioned to oversee the management of Yellowstone for 30 years between 1886 and 1916. In 1917, administration of the park was transferred to the National Park Service, which had been created the previous year. Hundreds of structures have been built and are protected for their architectural and historical significance, and researchers have examined more than a thousand archaeological sites.

Yellowstone National Park spans an area of 3,468.4 sq mi (8,983 km2), comprising lakes, canyons, rivers, and mountain ranges. Yellowstone Lake is one of the largest high-elevation lakes in North America and is centered over the Yellowstone Caldera, the largest super volcano on the continent. The caldera is considered a dormant volcano. It has erupted with tremendous force several times in the last two million years. Well over half of the world's geysers and hydrothermal features are in Yellowstone, fueled by this ongoing volcanism. Lava flows and rocks from volcanic eruptions cover most of the land area of Yellowstone. The park is the centerpiece of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the largest remaining nearly-intact ecosystem in the Earth's northern temperate zone. In 1978, Yellowstone was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Hundreds of species of mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, and amphibians have been documented, including several that are either endangered or threatened. The vast forests and grasslands also include unique species of plants. Yellowstone Park is the largest, and most famous megafauna location in the contiguous United States. Grizzly bears, cougars, wolves, and free-ranging herds of bison and elk live in this park. The Yellowstone Park bison herd is the oldest and largest public bison herd in the United States. Forest fires occur in the park each year; in the large forest fires of 1988, nearly one-third of the park was burnt. Yellowstone has numerous recreational opportunities, including hiking, camping, boating, fishing, and sightseeing. Paved roads provide close access to the major geothermal areas as well as some of the lakes and waterfalls. During the winter, visitors often access the park by way of guided tours that use either snow coaches or snowmobiles.

rbpo_response:
Okay, here’s a breakdown of whether a vegan diet is healthy for the average person, covering benefits and drawbacks:

**Generally, a well-planned vegan diet *can* be very healthy, but it requires careful attention to ensure adequate nutrient intake.**

**Potential Benefits:**

*   **Lower Risk of Chronic Diseases:** Studies consistently show vegans tend to have a lower risk of:
    *   **Heart Disease:** Lower cholesterol, blood pressure, and saturated fat intake.
    *   **Type 2 Diabetes:** Improved insulin sensitivity and blood sugar control.
    *   **Certain Cancers:** Higher fiber intake and antioxidant consumption may play a role.
    *   **Obesity:** Often lower in calories and higher in fiber, promoting fullness.
*   **Rich in Nutrients:** Vegan diets are naturally high in:
    *   **Fiber:** Promotes gut health, regularity, and satiety.
    *   **Vitamins & Minerals:** Abundant in fruits, vegetables, and legumes.
    *   **Antioxidants:** Protect cells from damage.
*   **Ethical & Environmental Considerations:** Many people choose veganism for animal welfare and environmental reasons.


**Potential Drawbacks & Considerations:**

*   **Nutrient Deficiencies (if not planned carefully):** This is the biggest concern. Vegans need to be mindful of:
    *   **Vitamin B12:** *Absolutely essential* to supplement or consume fortified foods. Deficiency leads to serious neurological problems.
    *   **Iron:** Plant-based iron (non-heme) is less readily absorbed than heme iron from animal sources. Combining with Vitamin C helps.
    *   **Omega-3 Fatty Acids:** Primarily found in fish. Vegans need to consume flaxseed, chia seeds, hemp seeds, or algae-based supplements.
    *   **Vitamin D:**  Supplementation is often recommended, especially in winter months or for those with limited sun exposure.
    *   **Calcium:**  Can be obtained from fortified plant milks and leafy greens, but needs to be prioritized.
    *   **Zinc:** Absorption can be inhibited by phytates in plant foods. Soaking or sprouting can help.
    *   **Protein:** While achievable, requires conscious effort to combine different plant sources to get all essential amino acids.
*   **Restrictive Eating:**  Can be socially challenging and require more meal planning.
*   **Potential for Unhealthy Vegan Foods:**  Vegan doesn’t automatically equal healthy.  Excessive processed vegan foods (vegan burgers, cheese, etc.) can be high in sodium, unhealthy fats, and additives.

**Important Note:**  It’s crucial to work with a registered dietitian or healthcare provider to ensure a vegan diet meets individual needs, especially if you have pre-existing health conditions.

    * **Study:** The Physicians Health Study (2003) showed that vegetarians had a 34% lower risk of type 2 diabetes than meat-eaters. ([https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12654887/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12654887/))
* **Weight Management:** Vegan diets tend to be lower in calories and higher in fiber, promoting satiety and potentially aiding weight loss or maintenance.
    * **Study:** A review in *The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* (2018) concluded that vegan diets can be effective for weight loss and maintenance. ([https://academic.oup.com/ajcn/article/108/3/655/4632328](https://academic.oup.com/ajcn/article/108/3/655/4632328))
* **Certain Cancers:** Higher consumption of fruits, vegetables, and fiber is associated with a lower risk of some cancers.
    * **Study:** The EPIC-Oxford study (2011) found that vegetarians had a lower risk of colorectal cancer. ([https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21466338/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21466338/))
* **Gut Health:** High fiber intake promotes a diverse and healthy gut microbiome.


**Potential Concerns & Considerations (Requires Careful Planning):**

* **Vitamin B12 Deficiency:**  B12 is primarily found in animal products. Vegans *must* supplement or consume fortified foods. Deficiency can lead to neurological problems.
    * **Study:**  Numerous studies demonstrate B12 deficiency in vegans without supplementation. ([https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6233338/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6233338/))
* **Iron Deficiency:** Plant-based iron (non-heme) is less readily absorbed than heme iron from animal sources.  Combining iron-rich foods with Vitamin C can improve absorption.
* **Omega-3 Fatty Acids:**  Vegans need to ensure adequate intake of ALA (alpha-linolenic acid) and potentially consider DHA/EPA supplementation (from algae).
* **Calcium & Vitamin D:**  Adequate intake from plant sources or supplementation is important for bone health.
* **Protein:** While achievable, vegans need to consciously include protein-rich plant foods like legumes, tofu, and nuts.

A very common and cherished Dutch tradition when a baby is born is the giving of a **"Kroegbiecht" (pub confession)**. Here’s a detailed explanation:

**What it is:**

A Kroegbiecht is a visit to a local pub (kroeg) shortly after the birth of a baby. The parents, along with close family and friends, go to the pub and confess their worries, anxieties, and hopes for the new baby to the bartender (the “biechtmeester”). 

**Historical Context & Origins:**

* **Catholic Roots:** This tradition stems from the Catholic Church’s practice of confession. During the Reformation, when Catholicism was suppressed in the Netherlands, the practice of confessing anxieties and fears to a trusted figure became a way to maintain a spiritual outlet.
* **Post-Reformation Adaptation:**  The "biechtmeester" in a pub stepped in as a secular substitute. The pub became a safe space to share concerns without judgment, mirroring the confessional.
* **Post-War Revival:**  The tradition truly gained popularity after World War II.  The war years were incredibly stressful, and people desperately needed a way to process their anxieties and celebrate new life amidst the hardship. The Kroegbiecht provided a communal and comforting ritual.

**The Process:**

1. **Timing:** Typically, the Kroegbiecht happens within the first few days or weeks after the birth.
2. **The Group:** Usually, a small group – often just the parents and a few close family members – attends.

bpo_response: Wine is an alcoholic beverage made from fermented grapes, where yeast converts sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide. Its style varies based on grape type, yeast strains, and the wine’s growing environment (terroir) and production methods. While primarily made from grapes, it can also be produced from other fruits. Legal appellations often regulate wine’s origin and production.
rbpo_response:
Here’s a detailed explanation of wine:

**What is Wine?**

Wine is an alcoholic beverage primarily made from the fermented juice of grapes. The process relies on yeast converting the natural sugars in the grapes into ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide. The “terroir” – encompassing the grape variety, climate, soil, and winemaking techniques – significantly impacts the final wine’s flavor and characteristics.

**Production Process:**

1.  **Harvesting:** Grapes are harvested when they reach optimal ripeness.
2.  **Crushing & Pressing:** Grapes are crushed to release the juice (must).  Some pressing may occur to extract more juice.
3.  **Fermentation:** Yeast is added to the must.  The yeast consumes the sugars, producing alcohol and carbon dioxide. This can happen in stainless steel tanks or oak barrels.
4.  **Aging:** Wine is aged in tanks or barrels to develop complexity and refine its flavors.
5.  **Bottling:**  The wine is filtered and bottled, ready for consumption.

**Types of Wine (Based on Grape & Style):**

*   **Red Wine:** Made from dark-skinned grapes, resulting in color and tannins. Examples: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinot Noir, Syrah.
*   **White Wine:** Made from green-skinned grapes or with the skins removed early. Examples: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling.
*   **Rosé Wine:** Made by brief contact of red grape skins with the juice, creating a pink color.
*   **Sparkling Wine:**  Wine with significant carbonation, often produced through the *méthode champenoise*. Examples: Champagne, Prosecco, Cava.

**Countries Producing Wine:**

Wine production is widespread globally, with major producing countries including:

*   **France:** Known for Bordeaux, Burgundy, Champagne, and Rhône wines.
*   **Italy:** Produces a vast array of styles, including Chianti, Barolo, and Prosecco.
*   **Spain:** Famous for Rioja, Sherry, and Priorat.
*   **United States:** California is a major producer, alongside Oregon and Washington.
*   **Australia:** Renowned for Shiraz and Chardonnay.
*   **Argentina:** Primarily known for Malbec.
*   **Portugal:** Produces Port and Vinho Verde.
*   **Germany:** Famous for Riesling wines.

**Appellations of Origin:**

Many countries have legal systems (appellations) that regulate wine production, defining where grapes can be grown and how wine can be made, ensuring quality and authenticity.

ori_prompt: What kind of method is Transfer printing
expected_response:
Transfer printing is a method of decorating pottery or other materials using an engraved copper or steel plate from which a monochrome print on paper is taken which is then transferred by pressing onto the ceramic piece. Pottery decorated using the technique is known as transferware or transfer ware.

It was developed in England from the 1750s on, and in the 19th century became enormously popular in England, though relatively little used in other major pottery-producing countries. The bulk of production was from the dominant Staffordshire pottery industry. America was a major market for English transfer-printed wares, whose imagery was adapted to the American market; several makers made this almost exclusively.

The technique was essential for adding complex decoration such as the Willow pattern to relatively cheap pottery. In particular, transfer printing brought the price of a matching dinner service low enough for large numbers of people to afford.

Apart from pottery, the technique was used on metal, and enamelled metal, and sometimes on wood and textiles. It remains used today, although mostly superseded by lithography. In the 19th century methods of transfer printing in colour were developed.

**Origin & History:**

* **Developed by SoundCloud (2012):** SoundCloud needed a robust system to monitor their rapidly scaling infrastructure. Existing solutions weren't sufficient.
* **Inspired by Google’s Borg:** Prometheus was heavily influenced by Google’s internal Borg monitoring system, but designed to be open-source and more accessible.
* **Open-sourced (2016):**  Released under the Apache License 2.0, making it freely available for anyone to use and contribute to.


**Purpose:**

Prometheus’s primary purpose is to collect and store metrics from monitored systems and applications, and then provide a powerful query language (PromQL) to analyze those metrics and generate alerts when specific conditions are met.  Essentially, it helps you understand the *health* and *performance* of your systems.

**Key Features:**

* **Pull-Based Model:**  Unlike push-based monitoring systems, Prometheus *pulls* metrics from targets (servers, services, etc.) at regular intervals. This is generally considered more efficient and less intrusive.
* **Time-Series Database:** Prometheus stores metrics as time-series data – meaning data points are associated with a timestamp. This is crucial for analyzing trends and patterns over time.
* **PromQL (Prometheus Query Language):**  A powerful query language specifically designed for analyzing time-series data. It allows you to:
    * Aggregate data
    * Calculate rates and averages
    * Filter data based on time ranges and labels
    * Create complex queries to understand system behavior.
* **Service Discovery:** Prometheus can automatically discover targets to monitor using various service discovery mechanisms (e.g., Kubernetes, Consul, DNS).
* **Alerting:**  Prometheus can define alerting rules based on PromQL expressions. When a rule is triggered, it sends alerts to various notification channels (e.g., email, Slack, PagerDuty).
* **Exporters:**  Prometheus doesn't monitor everything itself.  "Exporters" are applications that expose metrics in a format Prometheus understands.  Examples include:
    * **Node Exporter:** Monitors system-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk I/O) on servers.
    * **Blackbox Exporter:**  Monitors external services by sending HTTP requests and analyzing the responses.
* **Grafana Integration:** Prometheus integrates seamlessly with Grafana, a popular data visualization tool, allowing you to create dashboards to visualize your metrics.


**In short:** Prometheus is a flexible, powerful, and widely adopted tool for monitoring and alerting in modern, dynamic environments.

There are several boat classes in which athletes may compete, ranging from single sculls, occupied by one person, to shells with eight rowers and a coxswain, called eights. There are a wide variety of course types and formats of racing, but most elite and championship level racing is conducted on calm water courses 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) long with several lanes marked using buoys.

ori_prompt: Who invented the Jeans
context:
Jeans are a type of pants or trousers made from denim or dungaree cloth. Often the term "jeans" refers to a particular style of trousers, called "blue jeans", with copper-riveted pockets which were invented by Jacob W. Davis in 1871 and patented by Jacob W. Davis and Levi Strauss on May 20, 1873. Prior to the patent, the term "blue jeans" had been long in use for various garments (including trousers, overalls, and coats), constructed from blue-colored denim.

"Jean" also references a (historic) type of sturdy cloth commonly made with a cotton warp and wool weft (also known as "Virginia cloth"). Jean cloth can be entirely cotton as well, similar to denim. Originally designed for miners, modern jeans were popularized as casual wear by Marlon Brando and James Dean in their 1950s films, particularly The Wild One and Rebel Without a Cause, leading to the fabric becoming a symbol of rebellion among teenagers, especially members of the greaser subculture. From the 1960s onwards, jeans became common among various youth subcultures and subsequently young members of the general population. Nowadays, they are one of the most popular types of specialty trousers in Western culture. Historic brands include Levi's, Lee, and Wrangler.

Differential equations arise in many areas of science and technology, specifically whenever a deterministic relation involving some continuously varying quantities (modelled by functions) and their rates of change in space or time (expressed as derivatives) is known or postulated. This is illustrated in classical mechanics, where the motion of a body is described by its position and velocity as the time value varies. Newton's laws allow one (given the position, velocity, acceleration and various forces acting on the body) to express these variables dynamically as a differential equation for the unknown position of the body as a function of time. In some cases, this differential equation (called an equation of motion) may be solved explicitly.

context:
C++ (/ˈsiː plʌs plʌs/, pronounced "C plus plus") is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup. First released in 1985 as an extension of the C programming language, it has since expanded significantly over time; modern C++ currently has object-oriented, generic, and functional features, in addition to facilities for low-level memory manipulation. It is almost always implemented as a compiled language, and many vendors provide C++ compilers, including the Free Software Foundation, LLVM, Microsoft, Intel, Embarcadero, Oracle, and IBM.

C++ was designed with systems programming and embedded, resource-constrained software and large systems in mind, with performance, efficiency, and flexibility of use as its design highlights. C++ has also been found useful in many other contexts, with key strengths being software infrastructure and resource-constrained applications, including desktop applications, video games, servers (e.g. e-commerce, web search, or databases), and performance-critical applications (e.g. telephone switches or space probes).

C++ is standardized by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), with the latest standard version ratified and published by ISO in December 2020 as ISO/IEC 14882:2020 (informally known as C++20). The C++ programming language was initially standardized in 1998 as ISO/IEC 14882:1998, which was then amended by the C++03, C++11, C++14, and C++17 standards. The current C++20 standard supersedes these with new features and an enlarged standard library. Before the initial standardization in 1998, C++ was developed by Stroustrup at Bell Labs since 1979 as an extension of the C language; he wanted an efficient and flexible language similar to C that also provided high-level features for program organization. Since 2012, C++ has been on a three-year release schedule with C++23 as the next planned standard.
